title: Voz pasiva: Cortés y el Imperio mexica

sections.content: Ser + participle names what happened to someone or something, and often who did it with por — a natural fit for military narration where the focus is on who was captured, expelled, or executed. These sentences are taken directly from the previous reading.

items.spanish: El 8 de noviembre de 1519, Cortés fue recibido pacíficamente por el emperador Moctezuma II.
items.english: On November 8, 1519, Cortés was received peacefully by Emperor Moctezuma II.

items.spanish: Moctezuma poco después fue tomado como rehén dentro de su propio palacio.
items.english: Moctezuma was shortly afterward taken hostage inside his own palace.

items.spanish: Los españoles fueron expulsados violentamente de la ciudad, sufriendo enormes pérdidas.
items.english: The Spanish were violently expelled from the city, suffering huge losses.

items.spanish: Tenochtitlan finalmente fue conquistada el 13 de agosto de 1521.
items.english: Tenochtitlan finally fell (was conquered) on August 13, 1521.

sections.content: Passive voice puts the person or thing something happened TO in subject position (Cortés fue recibido...), which is exactly what a narrative needs when the receiver of the action matters more than the doer, or when the doer changes sentence to sentence. Compare it with active voice — Moctezuma recibió a Cortés — which shifts the emphasis entirely.
